Serum lipidomics in CIS versus MS: a site-confounded discovery analysis

Published

September 10, 2026

1 Summary

This report documents a discovery analysis of untargeted serum lipidomics data aimed at distinguishing Clinically Isolated Syndrome (CIS) from Multiple Sclerosis (MS). It covers the full pipeline: cohort construction, two independent feature-quality filters, correlation-based data reduction, penalised screening with false-discovery-rate control, and a bootstrap procedure that re-runs the entire pipeline in order to measure how much of the apparent result is optimism arising from having selected features on the same data.

The central finding is that one lipid feature (lip_727_65058_Da_672_95_s) is statistically robust in the pooled cohort, surviving a permutation test that corrects for 147 correlated tests while preserving the recruiting-centre structure. Its practical contribution, however, is small: adding the lipids to a model already containing centre, age and sex improves discrimination by less than four points on the C-index (Concordance Index). The reason is that the association is concentrated almost entirely at one centre — Eginitio, which contributes 20 of the 29 CIS patients. Within that centre alone the same feature is highly stable and strongly discriminating, but that analysis is exploratory, its effect size is inflated by selection, and no independent sample remains against which to validate it.

NoteReproducibility

All numbers in this document are read from three saved result objects. Two are produced by the analysis scripts (ms_lipidomics_pipeline11.R and ms_lipidomics_pipeline9_EginitioOnly.R); the third (ms_lipidomics_results_supplementary.rds) holds the permutation nulls, per-stratum fits, covariate-only baselines, the Site × lipid interaction test and the freeze-thaw degradation analysis, which span cohorts and so belong to neither pipeline. Nothing is transcribed and no model is refitted here: every table, figure and reported statistic is derived from those objects, including the candidate feature’s identity, which is read from the surviving feature name rather than hard-coded.

2 Study design and cohort construction

Exclusions

The analysis cohort was constructed by removing three groups, each for a reason established before any lipid was examined.

Cohort construction
Step n Reason
Full dataset 193 —
Drop AUTH batch1 143 Freeze-thaw degradation; retained as a technically compromised replication set
Drop healthy controls 128 Off-question for CIS-vs-MS; n=15, 73% from one centre
Drop Larissa 113 MS patients only — zero within-site information, causes complete separation

A note on the distinction between Larissa and the sparse-CIS centres: Larissa contained no CIS patients, so it carries no information at all about the contrast and a site indicator becomes a perfect predictor, making it impossible for the model to measure the actual biological effect. Attikon and AUTH batch2 contain few CIS patients, which is a different situation: they are underpowered for detection (i.e. cannot reliably detect small or subtle biological signals) but adequately powered for refutation of a large effect (i.e. seeing no huge effect in these groups allowed to confidently rule out an unlikely chance occurence or a major error). Because large biases could be ruled out even in centers with very few patients, the overall results are genuine rather than an artifact of which hospital collected the data.

Group composition by centre

Site × Group composition (analysis cohort, n = 113)
Eginitio supplies 20 of 29 CIS patients (69%)
Site CIS MS CIS share of that site
Eginitio 20 23 47%
Attikon 4 30 12%
AUTH_batch2 5 31 14%

This table indicates the Site confounding issue. The CIS-versus-MS contrast is, to a first approximation, an Eginitio-versus-elsewhere contrast. Nearly 70% of all CIS patients in the study (20 out of 29) came from a single hospital—Eginitio. Meanwhile, the other two hospitals supplied overwhelmingly MS patients. Because the patient types are divided this way, comparing CIS vs. MS is practically the same as comparing Eginitio Hospital vs. Other Hospitals. If Eginitio handled its blood samples slightly differently (such as using a different tube, a different freezer temperature, or a different processing time), that routine hospital quirk would show up almost exclusively in the CIS group. A harmless lab difference could easily trick someone into thinking it was a biological marker of the disease. To prevent hospital habits from masquerading as biological discoveries, the analysis was therefore centre-adjusted.

Effective sample size and the degrees-of-freedom budget

With a binary outcome, the information available is governed by the smaller class. Harrell’s effective sample size is \(n - (n_1^3 + n_0^3)/n^2\):

Effective sample size
The minority class is the binding constraint
Analysis n CIS MS Effective n df budget (n/20 – n/10)
Primary 113 29 84 64.7 3.2 – 6.5
Eginitio 43 20 23 32.1 1.6 – 3.2

This budget is the reason every downstream choice is conservative: one lipid screened at a time, penalised final models, and no interaction terms.

3 Feature processing

Two independent quality filters

Of 1,353 detected lipid features, 232 survived two filters that test different things and must both be applied.

Retention-time / mass filter (method-based, data-independent). Feature names encode accurate mass and retention time. A substantial fraction of features fell in the void volume (RT < 30 s, the solvent front) or the post-gradient wash (RT > 950 s) i.e. unretained contaminants and background ions rather than lipids.

Within-site detection filter (≥ 90% at every centre). Detection consistency alone is not sufficient evidence that a feature is an analyte: background ions are often detected in every sample precisely because they are systematic contamination. In this dataset 294 features passed detection filtering while sitting in the junk retention-time zone, so applying only one filter would have retained them.

Attikon detection fingerprint

Importance of stratifying the detection filter by centre:

An investigation of features whose detection was mutually exclusive across samples (74 pairs, against a permutation null with a maximum of 2) found that clustering samples on those features produced a clean group of 29 samples, all from Attikon. This looks like a pre-analytical difference — collection tube, clotting time, storage, or extraction — not biology, and it does not seem to be analytical drift: injection order was randomised across centres, and within-Eginitio run order does not predict group (p = 0.40).

In other words, Attikon had an unusual pattern. We noticed 74 pairs of chemical signals that were mutually exclusive i.e. if Signal A was present, Signal B was never there. By random chance, one would expect at most 2 such pairs. Then, grouping samples based on these signals revealed that 29 samples stood completely apart from all others and that every single one of those came from Attikon hospital. This wasn’t because Attikon’s patients were biologically unique. It was a “pre-analytical” difference—meaning it stemmed from how the samples were handled before reaching the lab (such as using a different brand of blood collection tube, a different clotting time, or different freezer storage). Also, because samples from different centers were analyzed in a randomized order, instrument drift or testing day variations could not explain the pattern.

Because the affected features would have appeared, in an unadjusted screen, as MS-enriched (Attikon being 4 CIS / 30 MS), a within-site detection threshold was adopted, and the idea of using detection status itself as a binary predictor was abandoned.

Data reduction by correlation clustering

Due to heavy collinearity, features were grouped by observed-only Spearman correlation and each cluster represented by its most central member.

ImportantClustering used observed values only

An early diagnostic showed that imputing below-detection values before clustering inflated the similarity of feature pairs that shared missing samples: co-missingness raised post-imputation similarity by roughly 0.0065 ρ per shared missing sample (t = 22.7), with the effect reaching ~0.06 ρ for the most co-missing pairs. Since missingness was itself site-structured, this would have produced clusters encoding centre rather than biology. Clustering was therefore performed on pairwise-complete rank correlations of observed values only, and imputation confined to the modelling step.

Data-reduction settings
Complete linkage at h = 0.50 guarantees |ρ| ≥ 0.71 for every within-cluster pair
Parameter Primary Eginitio
Detection threshold 0.90 per site 0.90
Features retained 232 322
Similarity Spearman ρ² Spearman ρ²
Linkage complete complete
Cut height (1 − ρ²) 0.50 0.50
Representatives 147 240
Named lipids among representatives 47 78

The cut height parameter was selected on outcome-blind criteria only such as cluster count, proportion of features in genuine (non-singleton) clusters, and largest cluster size, at the point beyond which maximum cluster size grows abruptly i.e. we gradually relaxed the parameter to group as many features as possible, but stopped just before having a “mega-cluster” that can contain unrelated features.

NoteHierarchical Clustering Linkage

The complete linkage method can be briefly described as follows: two groups are only merged if the two least similar items between them are still similar enough. This ensures every feature inside a cluster is tightly related to every other feature in that cluster.

4 Statistical approach

Screening

Each cluster representative was tested for association with Group, adjusting for centre, age and sex:

\[ \text{logit}\,P(\text{MS}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{Site} + f(\text{Age}) + \beta_3\text{Gender} + \beta_4\,\text{lipid}_j \]

with the lipid entering linearly on the \(\log_2\) scale (so a coefficient is an odds ratio per doubling of abundance), and Benjamini–Hochberg control across representatives.

Fitting used Firth’s penalised likelihood rather than ordinary maximum likelihood. With 29 CIS patients, unpenalised fits can separate i.e. the estimate diverges, the deviance goes to zero, and the feature would go through FDR as a false discovery. Firth guarantees finite estimates, and unlike ridge penalties its penalised profile likelihood ratio test retains a valid \(\chi^2\) reference distribution, so its \(p\)-values remain legitimate inputs to FDR.

NoteVerification of test calibration

Permuting Group within centre and re-running the screen 400 times gave a rejection rate of 0.0503 at \(\alpha = 0.05\) i.e. essentially exact. Permuting freely (breaking the Group–Site association as well) gave 0.0402, i.e. mildly conservative, confirming that the within-site permutation is the correct null.

Penalisation of the final model

The combined model containing surviving lipids was penalised by bisecting a single ridge parameter to a target effective degrees of freedom, fitting penalised from the first call. This mattered because an earlier version selected the penalty from an unpenalised starting fit, which failed in 18% of bootstrap replicates when the number of survivors approached the sample size.

Targets were derived from an AICc trace on each full-data model and, in the Eginitio analysis, checked against calibration.

Bootstrapping Procedure

Reported performance is corrected for optimism using 400 bootstrap replicates in which the entire pipeline is re-run: detection filtering, similarity computation, clustering, representative selection, imputation, screening, FDR, and model fitting. Only the fixed, outcome-blind constants (retention-time window, detection threshold, cut height, model formula) are held constant.

This distinction is quantitatively large. Validating only the fixed final model with rms::validate gives a Dxy optimism of 0.082; wrapping the whole pipeline gives 0.145. The difference of 0.063 in Dxy is the cost of having screened 147 representatives, and it would have been invisible to any procedure that treats the selected features as pre-specified.

Incrementing over the covariate skeleton

Corrected C-index: covariates alone versus covariates plus lipids
Both figures optimism-corrected, so the comparison is like-for-like
Analysis Covariate model C (covariates only) C (with lipids) Increment
Primary Site + rcs(Age,3) + Gender 0.721 0.760 0.038
Eginitio Age + Gender 0.573 0.883 0.309

In the primary analysis the lipids add less than four points of C-index over centre, age and sex. Centre is doing nearly all of the discriminating. In the Eginitio analysis, where there is no centre term, the covariate model is barely better than chance and the lipid does almost all of the work.

CautionComparison asymmetry

The covariate-only model is bootstrapped without a selection step, while the full model’s correction absorbs the feature selection screening. The increment is therefore conservative and the lipid model is held to the stricter standard i.e. the increment improvements could be an under-statement.

Calibration

Two models are fitted in every bootstrap replicate and both are shown above. They answer different questions and are not interchangeable:

  • The inferential model keeps Site. Its job is to give lipid coefficients that are not contaminated by centre effects, and it is the model behind every effect estimate reported here. It cannot be deployed, because a fitted Site factor with three levels has no column for a patient from a fourth hospital.
  • The prediction model drops Site. Its job is to be usable somewhere else. Its coefficients should not be read as effect sizes, since with Site removed they absorb some of the between-centre variation.

The features entering the two are identical — the screening step is the same, and Site is only dropped afterwards — so any difference between the panels is attributable to the Site term and the shrinkage alone.

The reported curve in each panel is the pooled out-of-sample curve: each replicate’s model scored on the original data. This is already a held-out quantity and requires no optimism correction.

NoteNot using the classic bias-corrected curve

The standard estimator, apparent − mean(train − test), assumes in-sample calibration is optimistic and produces the classic bias-corrected curve. That assumption fails for a penalised selection pipeline. Replicate models carry between one and thirty survivors, so reaching a fixed effective-df target requires very different amounts of shrinkage; their median apparent calibration slope was 1.48, against 1.05 for the full-data model which has a single survivor. Heavily shrunk models are under-dispersed in-sample, so train − test came out negative and the “correction” pushed the curve away from the diagonal. This seems to be a general property of bootstrapping penalised selection.

6 Site-heterogeneity

Leave-one-site-out and per-stratum estimates

Per-stratum Firth estimates for the candidate feature
Unadjusted within-stratum fits
Stratum CIS MS log OR OR 95% CI
Eginitio 20 23 -3.073 0.046 0.005 – 0.185
Attikon 4 30 0.054 1.056 0.248 – 1.688
AUTH_batch2 5 31 0.138 1.147 0.541 – 1.823
AUTH_batch1 13 34 -0.572 0.564 0.084 – 3.620

Heterogeneity is substantial and statistically significant: \(I^2 = 74.7\%\), \(\tau^2 = 1.51\), Cochran’s \(Q = 11.84\) on 3 df, \(p = 0.008\). A formal Site × lipid interaction test in the pooled model agreed i.e. \(\chi^2 = 14.92\), 2 df, \(p = 5.8\times 10^{-4}\).

The prediction interval (red horizontal bar) denotes the plausible odds ratio at an unsampled centre. It spans 0.005 to 44.5. This indicates that the selected feature can not be reliably used at a fourth new hospital.

WarningForest plot interpretation

Three of the four strata (Eginitio, Attikon, AUTH batch2) are the samples from which this feature was selected, so decomposing that result by centre generates no new evidence. Only AUTH batch1 is independent of the selection step, and it was inconclusive: OR 0.56 (0.09 – 3.69), with roughly 38% power against the pooled effect (the effect pointed the same way but the confidence interval was wide enough to include no effect at all).

Sparse centres

Attikon and AUTH batch2 have wide confidence intervals and cannot establish whether a modest effect is present there. They can, however, rule out an effect of the magnitude seen at Eginitio: the gap between Eginitio’s estimate and AUTH batch2’s is roughly ten standard errors. Their usefulness was never in finding something; it was in showing that what was found elsewhere does not appear there.

7 Eginitio-only analysis (exploratory)

ImportantExploratory analysis

The Eginitio stratum was selected after observing the site-stratified results. The inclusion criterion, that strata contributing fewer than ten CIS patients cannot support a centre-specific coefficient, depends only on the Site × Group composition, which was fixed at recruitment and known before any lipid was examined. Nevertheless, the rule was formulated post hoc, and no \(p\)-value or confidence interval reported in this section has its nominal coverage (i.e. should be read as if it had been planned from the start).

There is no Site term at a single centre, so unlike the primary analysis these two panels do not contrast Site-in against Site-out. They contrast two amounts of shrinkage applied to the same model, fitted to the same lipid.

The two therefore rank patients almost identically — corrected discrimination differs by less than two hundredths — and disagree only about how confidently that ranking should be translated into probabilities. The upper panel is shrunk harder, which yields more conservative coefficients at the cost of predictions that are systematically too cautious: its calibration slope is 1.72, meaning the observed frequencies rise faster than the predicted ones. The lower panel is shrunk less and its slope is 1.04, so its predicted probabilities can be read at face value.

The upper is the model behind any effect estimate, the lower is the model behind any predicted probability.

Discrimination is insensitive to the penalty across the range explored (corrected C between 0.876 and 0.893) while calibration is not: the calibration slope moves from 1.72 at an effective df of 2.5, through 1.34 at the AICc optimum of 3.17, to 1.04 at 4.0, with mean absolute calibration error halving over the same range. The choice of penalty was therefore made on calibration.

Effect size

The reported effect comes from the Firth linear fit, which is the model the screen actually used, has no evidence of nonlinearity (shape test \(p = 0.80\)), and yields a profile-likelihood interval:

Candidate feature effect size, Eginitio only
Higher abundance is associated with CIS rather than MS
Quantity Value
OR per doubling of abundance 0.042 (95% CI 0.0039 – 0.186)
OR over the observed interquartile range (1.54 doublings) 0.0076
Unpenalised (ML) estimate for comparison 0.018
Firth shrinkage of the log-odds 21%
Median log2 abundance, CIS 14.7 (IQR 14.4 – 14.8)
Median log2 abundance, MS 13.2 (IQR 12.8 – 13.5)

The magnitude is unusually large for a serum lipid, and the reason is visible in the raw distributions: the interquartile ranges of the two groups do not overlap at this centre. The odds ratio is large because the groups barely overlap on this measurement, not because a small shift produces a huge effect.

CautionTwo distinct biases

Firth corrects bias arising from sparse data; the estimate moved from 0.018 to 0.042, a 21% reduction in the log-odds. It does nothing about bias arising from selection. The reported figure is therefore a sparsity-corrected estimate of a coefficient that remains selection-inflated, and its confidence interval conditions on the feature having been chosen as the best of 240 candidates.

Sub-threshold features

Twenty features reached nominal \(p \le 0.05\) in the Eginitio screen against a permutation-null median of 8 — an excess of roughly 2–4× that is consistent across every tail threshold tested, but which does not reach significance (\(p \approx 0.06\), Monte Carlo SE ≈ 0.012 at 400 permutations). Their per-feature permutation \(p\)-values match their asymptotic values closely, so the enrichment is not a calibration artefact; the features are simply weak.

8 Technical quality control

Freeze-thaw degradation in AUTH batch1

AUTH batch1 was excluded from discovery and its degradation characterised directly. Both AUTH batches were analysed in the same instrument sequence, so everything downstream of the freezer was identical, making the comparison a clean natural experiment. The comparison was restricted to MS patients so that group composition cannot explain it.

Product-to-substrate ratios, AUTH batch1 vs batch2
MS patients only
metric batch1 batch2 p_value direction
LPC / PC (median ratio) 0.3395937 0.2140305 2.804034e-12 product enriched in batch1
DG / TG (median ratio) 1.6828282 1.3539890 1.710382e-01 product enriched in batch1

Every substrate class is depleted in batch1 (PE, PC, PI, CE, SM) and every hydrolysis product enriched (LPC, DG, Cer) i.e. phosphatidylcholine loses a chain to become lysophosphatidylcholine, triacylglycerol becomes diacylglycerol, sphingomyelin becomes ceramide (Ishikawa et al. 2014; Reis et al. 2021).

That pattern is suggestive but not decisive on its own, because the two batches are different patients. Phospholipase A2 is active in vivo as well as in a freezer, so a group of patients with more inflammation would also show a raised product-to-substrate ratio. A test that a population difference cannot imitate is needed, and the enzyme’s positional chemistry supplies one.

Phosphatidylcholine has a glycerol backbone carrying a fatty acid at position sn-1, a second at sn-2, and a phosphocholine head group at sn-3. Phospholipase A2 cleaves specifically at sn-2, releasing that chain and leaving lysophosphatidylcholine behind (Khan and Ilies 2023; Mouchlis and Dennis 2019). Biology places these chains non-randomly: sn-1 typically carries a saturated fatty acid (16:0, 18:0) while sn-2 typically carries an unsaturated or polyunsaturated one (18:2, 20:4, 22:6) (Mouchlis and Dennis 2019). That asymmetry is maintained by the Lands cycle, in which phospholipids are deacylated and reacylated with different chains, preferentially incorporating polyunsaturated fatty acids (Jackson, Abate, and Tonks 2008). Double bonds are therefore concentrated at exactly the position the enzyme attacks.

Feature names give sum composition, PC_38_6 is 38 carbons and 6 double bonds across both chains, so a species with many double bonds must be carrying a polyunsaturated chain, almost certainly at sn-2. If phospholipase activity caused the depletion, the loss should therefore scale with double-bond count. A difference between two patient populations offers no reason for such a gradient to exist.

Double-bond specificity of the batch1 depletion
Rank correlation is of most importance: two outliers at db = 3 inflate the OLS residual variance
Class Species tested OLS slope OLS p Spearman rho Spearman p
PC (substrate) 21 -0.118 0.0888 -0.563 0.00781
LPC (product) 10 0.004 0.8150 0.151 0.67700

Polyunsaturated PC species are depleted more than saturated ones (Spearman \(\rho = -0.56\), \(p = 0.0078\)), which is the sn-2 positional specificity a phospholipase produces (Khan and Ilies 2023; Mouchlis and Dennis 2019) and which a difference between two patient populations would not generate.

The gradient is present on the substrate side. The product side is less tidy: LPC species are uniformly enriched (intercept +0.20, p = 0.0007) but show no double-bond trend. If cleavage were purely at sn-2 the retained sn-1 chain would usually be saturated, so enrichment should have concentrated among low-double-bond LPC species. Flat enrichment instead suggests either mixed phospholipase A1 and A2 activity, or that LPC is itself being consumed further by lysophospholipases, which would flatten the product profile.

NoteTwo caveats on the double-bond argument

Sum composition does not say which chain carries the double bonds (Liebisch et al. 2013, 2020), so double-bond count is a proxy for sn-2 unsaturation rather than a direct measure. And polyunsaturated species are also the most susceptible to autoxidation, which freeze-thawing likewise promotes; so the gradient alone is consistent with oxidation as well as hydrolysis. It is the simultaneous enrichment of LPC that points specifically at hydrolysis (Reis et al. 2021), since oxidation would not generate LPC.

NoteAttribution

The degradation itself is verified. Attributing it to freeze-thawing is an inference — in vivo phospholipase A2 activity produces the same signature — and rests on the known provenance of those samples rather than on the data.

The candidate feature itself differs between the two batches (\(p = 0.008\)) in the product direction, with preserved standard deviation. A location shift with unchanged spread is consistent with systematic chemical conversion rather than added noise, which is why AUTH batch1 cannot serve as a validation set for this particular feature.

Analytical identity of the candidate

Candidate feature and its cluster-mate
Both unannotated; retention times differ by 0.14 s
Feature m/z RT (s) RT (min) Role
lip_727_65058_Da_672_95_s 727.6506 672.95 11.22 FDR survivor
lip_682_59229_Da_673_09_s 682.5923 673.09 11.22 Cluster-mate; co-elutes

Both features are unannotated. They co-elute and are strongly correlated, which is why they cluster together, and the cluster is selected in approximately 75% of primary bootstrap replicates while which member represents it varies (52% and 24% respectively). Whether these represent one analyte detected as two ions or two co-eluting species is an analytical question requiring MS/MS spectra; it affects how the result should be reported.

9 Limitations

Limitations
Limitation Detail
Treatment confounding Disease-modifying therapy and recent corticosteroid exposure were not available. MS patients are typically treated and CIS patients are not, and several DMTs (S1P modulators, teriflunomide) act directly on lipid metabolism. Part of the signal may be a drug signature.
Post-hoc stratum selection The Eginitio-only analysis was chosen after observing where the effect appeared. Its p-values and intervals do not have nominal coverage.
Winner's curse The reported effect size is selection-inflated. Firth corrects sparse-data bias only; no correction for selection bias is applied to the point estimate.
No independent validation set AUTH batch1 is technically compromised and its test was underpowered. No untouched sample remains.
Cross-sectional design The data cannot support claims about conversion from CIS to MS, only about differences between prevalent groups.
Unannotated candidate The surviving feature has an accurate mass and retention time but no confirmed identity.
Fasting status Not standardised or recorded; serum lipids vary substantially with prandial state.

10 Conclusions

The serum lipidome differs across the CIS–MS spectrum in this cohort, but the difference is centre-dependent. One feature is statistically robust in the pooled data after correcting for multiplicity with a null that preserves the recruiting-centre structure, yet contributes less than four points of C-index beyond centre, age and sex. Within the single centre with balanced group sizes it is highly stable and strongly discriminating, but that analysis is exploratory, its effect size is inflated, and there is no independent sample left to check it against.

The defensible claim is that this feature shows a large, well-behaved association at one centre; that the association differs significantly across centres; and that the only independent sample was too small and too technically compromised to make a formal judgement. That is more of a hypothesis worth testing properly in a new cohort, not a claim of a biomarker.

Two additions would substantially strengthen the work: treatment and steroid exposure data, which could convert an unexplained centre effect into an explained one, and validation in a genuinely independent cohort with adequate CIS representation at more than one site.
